question: A multinational retailer has 400 projects under several folders. The CISO requires that SSH and RDP from the internet be blocked in every VPC, that project teams cannot override this control, and that project teams remain free to define their own additional firewall rules. What should you do?
options: Create a VPC firewall rule in each project that denies TCP ports 22 and 3389 from 0.0.0.0/0 with priority 0, and use Cloud Asset Inventory to detect deletions.
Create a hierarchical firewall policy at the organization node with high-priority deny rules for TCP 22 and 3389 from 0.0.0.0/0 followed by a goto_next rule, and associate it with the organization.
Create a global network firewall policy in each VPC with deny rules for TCP 22 and 3389 and restrict the Compute Security Admin role so teams cannot edit it.
Set the organization policy constraint compute.restrictProtocolForwardingCreationForTypes to block SSH and RDP across all projects.
explanation: Hierarchical firewall policies are evaluated before VPC-level rules and are inherited by every project under the organization or folder they are attached to, so a deny rule at the organization node cannot be overridden by project owners; a trailing goto_next rule delegates all other traffic decisions to lower-level policies and VPC firewall rules, preserving team autonomy. Option A is not enforceable because project owners can delete or modify project-level rules, and detection after the fact is not prevention. Option C is per-VPC and requires touching hundreds of networks and restricting IAM in each project, which is operationally heavy and still bypassable by anyone who can create VPCs. Option D references an organization policy constraint that governs protocol forwarding rules, not firewall traffic filtering. This is a security-pillar control applied at the highest point in the resource hierarchy.
hint: Core Rule: Hierarchical firewall policies are evaluated before VPC-level rules and are inherited by every project under the organization or folder they are attached to, so a deny rule at the organization node cannot be overridden by project owners; a trailing goto_next rule delegates all other traffic decisions to lower-level policies and VPC firewall rules, preserving team autonomy.

This aligns with the security pillar's guidance to prefer managed, layered network controls.

question: A banking app's /login endpoint, behind a global external Application Load Balancer, is being hit by credential-stuffing attacks from thousands of rotating source IPs, each sending a moderate number of requests. question: A SaaS company's security team discovered that developers can attach any network tag to their VMs and thereby match permissive VPC firewall rules intended for other tiers. The team wants firewall targeting that is governed by IAM so only authorized principals can assign a given tag to a VM, and it wants one policy that applies to multiple VPCs in a project. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Create Resource Manager tags (secure tags) with a Tag Administrator managing the keys and grant Tag User only to the principals allowed to bind each tag value.
Restrict the compute.instanceAdmin role so developers cannot edit network tags on running VMs.
Create a global network firewall policy that uses the secure tags in its target and source specifications, and associate the policy with each VPC network.
Convert the existing VPC firewall rules to use service accounts as targets, and give each developer a personal service account.
Enable Firewall Rules Logging on the permissive rules so misuse of tags can be audited.
explanation: Secure tags are Resource Manager tags with IAM-governed binding: only principals holding Tag User on a tag value can attach it to a VM, which closes the loophole where anyone with instance edit rights can add a network tag. Secure tags are supported only in network firewall policies, and a single global network firewall policy can be associated with multiple VPC networks, satisfying the reuse requirement. Option B does not work because network tag editing is part of normal instance management and cannot be separated cleanly. Option D substitutes service-account targeting, which is IAM-governed but is limited to the legacy VPC firewall rule model per network and does not scale well to one policy across VPCs; issuing personal service accounts is also an anti-pattern. Option E provides audit visibility but does not prevent the misuse. This is a least-privilege improvement under the security pillar.

question: A media company is creating a VPC-native GKE Standard cluster that must scale to 500 nodes with the default maximum of 110 Pods per node. Corporate IP space is scarce, so the network team wants the smallest secondary ranges that still allow the cluster to reach full size without recreating it. Which secondary range sizes should you plan for the Pod range?
options: A /16 Pod range, because it provides 65,536 addresses which exceeds 500 nodes x 110 Pods.
A /15 Pod range, because each node with 110 Pods is allocated a /24 and 500 nodes require more than the 256 /24 blocks that a /16 provides.
A /19 Pod range, because 500 nodes x 110 Pods is approximately 55,000 addresses and a /19 covers it with 33% headroom.
A /24 Pod range per node pool, because GKE allocates Pod addresses per node pool rather than per node.
explanation: GKE reserves a Pod CIDR block per node sized to twice the maximum Pods per node; with the default 110 Pods, each node receives a /24 (256 addresses). A /16 contains only 256 /24 blocks, so it caps the cluster at 256 nodes; 500 nodes need at least 500 /24 blocks, which requires a /15 (512 blocks). Option A and Option C make the common mistake of multiplying nodes by Pods without accounting for per-node block allocation. Option D is incorrect because allocation is per node, although you can add additional Pod ranges to node pools with discontiguous multi-Pod CIDR if you later run out. Alternatively, reducing max Pods per node to 64 or fewer would shrink each node's block to a /25 and allow a /16, but the question fixes the default. Correct CIDR planning is essential to avoid costly cluster re-creation.
hint: Core Rule (GKE networking): GKE reserves a Pod CIDR block per node sized to twice the maximum Pods per node; with the default 110 Pods, each node receives a /24 (256 addresses).

question: A manufacturer has migrated part of its application estate to a VPC connected to its factory data center via HA VPN. Workloads in the VPC must resolve hostnames in the internal on-premises domain corp.example.internal, which is served by Active Directory DNS servers. Create a Cloud DNS private zone for corp.example.internal and manually replicate the on-premises records with a scheduled script.
Create a Cloud DNS public zone for corp.example.internal and delegate it from the on-premises DNS servers.

question: A media company's platform team manages all private DNS records for internal.example.com in a Cloud DNS private zone attached to the Shared VPC host network. A data science team runs a standalone VPC in a different project, connected to the host network with VPC Network Peering, and its VMs cannot resolve internal.example.com names. The platform team must remain the single owner of the zone. What should you do?
options: Attach the existing private zone to the data science VPC as an additional authorized network.
Create a second private zone for internal.example.com in the data science project and copy the records nightly.
Create a Cloud DNS peering zone for internal.example.com in the data science VPC that targets the Shared VPC host network.
Enable custom route export on the VPC Network Peering so that DNS records are propagated to the peered network.
explanation: DNS peering lets one VPC (the consumer) forward lookups for a namespace to the DNS configuration of another VPC (the producer), so the data science VPC resolves internal.example.com using the host network's private zone without the platform team giving up ownership. Option A is technically possible for zones you control, but it requires the platform team to attach an external project's VPC to its zone and manage network lists as teams change; DNS peering delegates this cleanly and is the recommended cross-project pattern, and in some cases the consumer project cannot authorize itself. Option B creates duplicate data and drift. Option D is wrong because VPC peering exchanges routes, not DNS configuration; Cloud DNS private zones are never propagated across VPC peering. This preserves single ownership while enabling consumption, in line with the operational-excellence pillar.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud DNS): DNS peering lets one VPC (the consumer) forward lookups for a namespace to the DNS configuration of another VPC (the producer), so the data science VPC resolves internal.example.com using the host network's private zone without the platform team giving up ownership.

question: A government portal uses a Cloud DNS public managed zone for gov-services.example. A security audit requires protection against DNS cache-poisoning and spoofing attacks so that resolvers can cryptographically verify responses. What should you do?
options: Enable Cloud DNS query logging on the zone and alert on unexpected response patterns.
Enable DNSSEC on the managed zone, then add the generated DS record to the parent zone through the domain registrar.
Convert the zone to a private zone so that only VPC resolvers can query it.
Attach a Cloud Armor security policy to the zone to filter malicious DNS queries.
explanation: DNSSEC signs zone data so that validating resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity, defeating cache poisoning and spoofing. In Cloud DNS you enable DNSSEC on the zone, and the chain of trust is completed only after the DS record is published in the parent zone at the registrar, a step that is frequently forgotten. Option A provides visibility but no cryptographic protection. Option C would make the public portal's name unresolvable from the internet. Option D is not possible; Cloud Armor protects HTTP(S) load balancers and does not attach to DNS zones. DNSSEC is a standard security-pillar recommendation for public zones.
hint: Core Rule: DNSSEC signs zone data so that validating resolvers can verify authenticity and integrity, defeating cache poisoning and spoofing.

question: A logistics company runs a fleet of Compute Engine VMs without external IP addresses in a single subnet. The VMs must download OS updates from public repositories and call a partner's API that allowlists only two specific source IP addresses provided in advance. The company wants a managed solution. What should you do?
options: Create a Cloud NAT gateway on the subnet's Cloud Router, reserve two static external IP addresses, and configure the gateway with manual NAT IP allocation using those addresses.
Create a Cloud NAT gateway with automatic IP allocation and give the partner the IP range published by Google for the region.
Assign a static external IP address to each VM and configure VPC firewall rules to allow egress only to the partner and update repositories.
Deploy a Compute Engine VM as a NAT instance with two static external IPs and add a default route through it.
explanation: Cloud NAT is a managed, distributed NAT service that supports manual NAT IP allocation from reserved static external addresses, giving the partner a stable set of source IPs to allowlist while keeping the VMs private. Option B does not work because automatically allocated NAT IPs can change and Google does not publish a stable regional egress range for Cloud NAT. Option C violates the design principle of no external IPs on VMs and produces one IP per VM instead of the two agreed addresses. Option D is a self-managed single point of failure that requires patching and scaling, contrary to the managed-solution requirement. This favors the security and operational-excellence pillars.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud NAT is a managed, distributed NAT service that supports manual NAT IP allocation from reserved static external addresses, giving the partner a stable set of source IPs to allowlist while keeping the VMs private.

question: A web-scraping analytics startup runs 200 Compute Engine VMs behind a Cloud NAT gateway. Applications intermittently fail with connection timeouts to a small set of external APIs, and Cloud NAT logs show dropped_sent_packet errors with reason OUT_OF_RESOURCES. Cloud Monitoring shows the gateway has spare NAT IP addresses. What is the most likely cause and the recommended fix?
options: The NAT gateway is regional and traffic crosses regions; create a Cloud NAT gateway in each region where VMs run.
The subnet is not enabled for Cloud NAT; edit the gateway to include all subnet IP ranges.
The gateway lacks external IP addresses; switch from manual to automatic NAT IP allocation.
VMs are exhausting their allocated source ports to the same destination IP:port pairs; enable dynamic port allocation and raise the maximum ports per VM, or increase the minimum ports per VM.
explanation: Cloud NAT assigns each VM a fixed number of source ports (64 by default); connections from one VM to the same destination IP and port must use distinct source ports, so VMs talking heavily to a few APIs exhaust their allocation and Cloud NAT drops new connections with OUT_OF_RESOURCES even when spare NAT IPs exist. Enabling dynamic port allocation lets Cloud NAT grow a VM's ports between a minimum and maximum on demand, or you can raise the static minimum ports per VM. Option A is wrong because Cloud NAT serves VMs in its own region, and a mismatch would cause complete failure rather than intermittent drops. Option B would produce no connectivity at all for the subnet, not intermittent timeouts. Option C contradicts the observation that IP addresses are not exhausted. Understanding port allocation is key to Cloud NAT reliability tuning.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud NAT assigns each VM a fixed number of source ports (64 by default); connections from one VM to the same destination IP and port must use distinct source ports, so VMs talking heavily to a few APIs exhaust their allocation and Cloud NAT drops new connections with OUT_OF_RESOURCES even when spare NAT IPs exist.

question: An enterprise runs an internal HTTP microservice on GKE clusters in us-central1 and europe-west1. Internal clients in both regions and in on-premises sites must call a single private hostname, be routed to the closest healthy region, and fail over automatically if one region is down. Traffic must never leave Google's network. Which load balancer should you use?
options: Two regional internal Application Load Balancers with a Cloud DNS routing policy that uses geolocation to steer clients between regional IPs.
A cross-region internal Application Load Balancer with backends in both regions, using a proxy-only subnet in each region and a private DNS name pointing to its forwarding rules.
A global external Application Load Balancer with backends in both regions, restricted to internal source IPs using Cloud Armor.
An internal passthrough Network Load Balancer in each region with global access enabled and round-robin DNS between the two addresses.
explanation: The cross-region internal Application Load Balancer is an Envoy-based Layer 7 load balancer that is reachable only from internal and hybrid clients, spans multiple regions, routes clients to the nearest healthy backends, and automatically fails over to another region, all without leaving Google's network. Option A can approximate this with DNS geolocation and health-checked routing policies, but DNS-based failover is slower, subject to client caching, and requires operating two separate load balancers and URL maps. Option C sends traffic through public-facing front ends, contradicting the requirement that traffic stay private, and Cloud Armor allowlisting is not a substitute for internal exposure. Option D is Layer 4, so it lacks HTTP routing, and round-robin DNS has no health awareness. This is the reliability-pillar choice for multi-region internal services.
hint: Core Rule (Internal load balancing): The cross-region internal Application Load Balancer is an Envoy-based Layer 7 load balancer that is reachable only from internal and hybrid clients, spans multiple regions, routes clients to the nearest healthy backends, and automatically fails over to another region, all without leaving Google's network.

question: A conglomerate is designing the IP address plan for a new Shared VPC that will connect to three on-premises data centers over Dedicated Interconnect and will host GKE clusters, Cloud SQL private IP instances, and internal load balancers. Which two practices should you follow when allocating subnet ranges? (Choose two.)
options: Use the same 10.0.0.0/8 ranges already assigned on-premises, because Cloud Router will translate overlapping prefixes.
Reserve contiguous, non-overlapping blocks for each region and environment from a central IPAM, leaving room for GKE secondary ranges, proxy-only subnets, and private services access allocations.
Create subnets as small as possible now and plan to shrink or re-create them later if the estimate proves wrong.
Size primary subnet ranges generously, since a subnet's primary range can be expanded later but never shrunk, and avoid CIDR blocks that conflict with Google's reserved or restricted ranges.
Use one large /8 subnet in a single region for simplicity and rely on firewall rules for segmentation.
explanation: Sound VPC IP planning requires that cloud ranges never overlap on-premises ranges (BGP does not perform NAT, so overlapping prefixes are unreachable) and that space is set aside up front for the many consumers of addresses beyond VMs: GKE Pod and Service secondary ranges, proxy-only subnets for Envoy-based load balancers, private services access ranges for Cloud SQL, and PSC endpoints. Subnet primary ranges can be expanded but not shrunk, so being generous with the primary range and reserving contiguous blocks per region and environment avoids future re-creation. Option A is wrong because Cloud Router does not translate addresses. Option C invites disruptive re-creation. Option E is a single-region, unsegmented design that defeats regional expansion and makes hybrid summarization impossible. Careful CIDR planning is a foundational reliability and operational-excellence practice.
hint: Core Rule (VPC design): Sound VPC IP planning requires that cloud ranges never overlap on-premises ranges (BGP does not perform NAT, so overlapping prefixes are unreachable) and that space is set aside up front for the many consumers of addresses beyond VMs: GKE Pod and Service secondary ranges, proxy-only subnets for Envoy-based load balancers, private services access ranges for Cloud SQL, and PSC endpoints.

question: A multiplayer game studio runs dedicated game servers on Compute Engine in us-west1. question: A streaming video service uses Cloud CDN in front of a global external Application Load Balancer with a Cloud Armor backend security policy that denies requests from embargoed countries. Auditors discovered that users in those countries can still download cached video segments. Why does this happen, and what should you do?
options: The backend security policy is in preview mode; switch the geo rule from preview to enforced.
Cloud CDN is not evaluating the security policy because CDN requires the rule to use request.headers['cf-ipcountry']; rewrite the rule accordingly.
The geo rule is being shadowed by a higher-priority allow rule; reorder the rule priorities in the backend security policy.

Backend security policies are only evaluated on cache misses; create a Cloud Armor edge security policy with the same geo-based deny rule and attach it to the CDN-enabled backend service so cache hits are also filtered.
explanation: Cloud Armor backend security policies are enforced when a request is forwarded to the backend, which means cache hits served by Cloud CDN bypass them entirely. Edge security policies are evaluated at the outer edge before the CDN cache lookup and support geo-based and IP-based filtering, so attaching an edge policy with the geo deny rule is the documented fix for filtering cached content. Option A could be a contributing misconfiguration but would allow all users, not only those receiving cached content, and the symptom (only cached objects leak) points to the cache path. Option B invents a header; Cloud Armor uses origin.region_code. Option C would also affect cache misses, so the symptom pattern would differ. Understanding where each control sits in the request path is central to the security pillar.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud Armor backend security policies are enforced when a request is forwarded to the backend, which means cache hits served by Cloud CDN bypass them entirely.
